clue.text: Note in constituency old rector and politician

indicators.note: in tells us the note sits inside the word for a constituency

parts.note: a seat is a parliamentary constituency, the place an MP is elected to represent
O is the abbreviation for old, as in OT for Old Testament
R is the abbreviation for rector, the clergyman in charge of a parish

explanation.surface: A memo records that the local electoral district holds an elderly clergyman and an elected member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts N inside SEAT, the British word for the district a Member of Parliament represents; 'and' only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of a senate, such as the upper house of the US Congress, is one example of an elected legislator.

clue.text: Promotion for energetic singer

indicators.note: to promote something is to move it up, so in a down entry the word that follows is written from the bottom upwards

parts.note: avid means keen and eager, pursuing something with vigour

explanation.surface: A publicity campaign is laid on for a lively vocalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Promotion for' is not publicity: promotion is a move upwards, which in a down entry means AVID is entered from the bottom up.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a celebrated female vocalist, especially an operatic soprano, so the word names one example of the type.

clue.text: Affectedly pretentious young man and woman

parts.note: a lad is a boy or youth
Ida is a woman's first name, standing in for any woman

explanation.surface: A youth and a lady are both putting on airs and graces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'woman' is one particular woman's name, a common crossword trick; 'and' simply joins the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a mocking informal adjective for someone with a showily refined, snobbish manner, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Spymaster is leading source of trouble

parts.note: M is the code name of the secret service head, James Bond's boss, in Ian Fleming's novels
taken as written
as an adjective chief means leading or principal, as in chief witness

explanation.surface: The head of an intelligence service turns out to be the main cause of the difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'source of trouble' looks like a first-letter instruction for T; it is the definition, and 'leading' is the adjective CHIEF.
explanation.definitionFit: The word can mean the cause of harm or annoyance, not just playful naughtiness, so it is a synonym for whatever brings bother.

clue.text: Tea top host arranged? Cleaning item required

indicators.note: arranged means put into order, so the letters of the three words before it are set out afresh

explanation.surface: A first-rate host has laid on tea, and something is needed for the clearing up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' reorders the letters of TEA TOP HOST, the question mark excusing the odd phrase; 'required' only says the answer is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the paste squeezed onto a brush for scrubbing teeth, an example of a product that cleans.

clue.text: Symbol of authority namely transforming Peter

parts.note: sc is short for the Latin scilicet, which means namely or that is to say

indicators.note: transforming means changing the form of something, so the letters of the name after it take a new order

explanation.surface: An emblem of power is singled out as the thing that is changing Peter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'namely' reads as a mere connective, but it supplies two letters itself, an abbreviation met mainly in footnotes and legal documents; 'transforming' then leaves the apostle's name as EPTRE.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the ornamental rod a monarch carries as an emblem of royal power, so it is an example.

clue.text: Clare playing retained appeal in musical performance

indicators.note: retained means kept hold of, so the reordered name keeps the word for appeal inside it
playing suggests the letters of the name are at play, moving into a new order

parts.note: it is an old informal word for sex appeal, as in the phrase 'It girl'

explanation.surface: Clare's playing kept its charm throughout the concert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' rearranges CLARE into RECAL, and 'retained' has that hold IT, the crossword standby for sex appeal; 'in' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a concert given by a soloist or small group, so it is an example of music played before listeners.

clue.text: Island backed account introduced by youngster

indicators.note: introduced by says the word for a youngster comes first, leading in the turned abbreviation

parts.note: a minor is a person below the age of legal adulthood

indicators.note: backed means sent backwards, so the abbreviation that follows is read from its end

parts.note: AC is a standard abbreviation for account, as on a bank statement

explanation.surface: An island lent its support to a story first presented by a child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' poses as 'supported' in the surface, but it turns a banking abbreviation into CA; 'introduced by' then sends the youngster to the front, though the clue mentions it last.
explanation.definitionFit: It is one of Spain's Balearic group in the Mediterranean, an example of land surrounded by sea.

clue.text: With nothing to do, vandalise a seat on dole

indicators.note: to vandalise is to wreck something, so the four words after it are broken up and their letters put back differently

explanation.surface: Bored and out of work, someone on benefits wrecks a bench.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vandalise' is an instruction to break up A SEAT ON DOLE; the dole is British slang for unemployment benefit, which gives the surface its idle vandal.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone idle and unoccupied, with no task in hand.

clue.text: Accepting lot getting a fact I misplaced about record

indicators.note: about means around, so the reordered letters go round the word for a record
misplaced means put in the wrong position, so the letters of the three words before it are moved around

parts.note: to list things is to record them, and a list is a written record of items

explanation.surface: While taking delivery of a batch, I mislaid a detail concerning a disc.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misplaced' rearranges A FACT I into FATAIC, and 'about' wraps that round LIST. 'lot' is one's fate, not a batch of goods; 'getting' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes someone resigned to destiny, which is what submitting to one's allotted portion in life amounts to.

clue.text: Sort dirty perfume bottles

indicators.note: as a verb, bottles means holds inside, so the two words before it contain the answer in consecutive letters

explanation.surface: Someone is told to go through a pile of grubby scent containers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottles' reads as a noun, the things to be sorted, but it is a verb: 'dirty perfume' holds the answer across the gap between its words.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are nouns for a kind or category of thing, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Game showing damaged boot in decline

indicators.note: in tells us the broken-up footwear goes inside the word for a decline

parts.note: a fall is a drop or decline, as in a fall in prices

indicators.note: damaged means broken, so the letters of the word after it are knocked out of order

explanation.surface: A match puts on show a battered boot that is well past its best.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'in decline' splits in two: 'in' is a placing instruction and 'decline' the noun it places things inside. 'damaged' leaves the footwear as OOTB; 'showing' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the team sport of kicking a ball at goals, an example of the general term.

clue.text: Appropriate drink? Male has drink with nothing in it

parts.note: a tot is a small measure of spirits, such as a nip of rum
he is the pronoun for a male person

indicators.note: in it says the nothing goes inside the second drink, the word just before

parts.note: a pint, the British pub measure of beer, is an everyday word for a drink of it
the letter O looks like zero, so it stands for nothing

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a beverage is suitable when the man has been served an empty glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate drink?' reads as one phrase, but only 'Appropriate' is the definition; the first 'drink' starts the wordplay and the second is a different one. 'in it' places the zero; 'has' and 'with' merely link.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means relevant and apt, a synonym for fitting the matter in hand.

clue.text: Convey meaning

definitions.meaning: as a verb, to signify or express a sense, the way words carry a message
as a noun, the significance or drift of what is said

explanation.definitionFit: One word is both a verb for signifying or expressing something and a noun for the significance of a statement, so each half is a synonym.

clue.text: Cold rugby player is beginning to hesitate

parts.note: the stand-off, also called the fly-half, is the rugby back who receives the ball from the scrum-half
taken as written

indicators.note: beginning to asks for just the opening letter of the word that follows it

explanation.surface: A chilly rugby player starts to waver out on the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby the stand-off (or fly-half) is the back who links the scrum-half to the three-quarters; 'beginning to' takes the H of 'hesitate'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe a person who is aloof and unfriendly in manner, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Wealthy figure I inspired — with unknown excellence

parts.note: nob is British slang for a rich or upper-class person
taken as written
to inspire a feeling is to kindle it, and what has been kindled has been lit
Y is one of the letters algebra uses for an unknown quantity

explanation.surface: A rich person I once encouraged turned out to have unsuspected greatness.
explanation.walkthrough: A nob is British slang for someone rich or upper-class. 'inspired' gives LIT in the sense of kindled or fired up; 'with' just joins on the algebraic Y.
explanation.definitionFit: As a quality of character it means high moral worth or grandeur, a synonym for outstanding merit.

clue.text: A late form of service?

parts.note: late here means dead rather than behind time, and the service is a religious ceremony, so this is the rite held for someone who has died

explanation.surface: A church service that takes place unusually late in the day.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the ceremony held to mark a death, 'late' being the polite word for deceased, so the whole phrase is a playful description.

clue.text: Ill-tempered agent consuming drink heading north

indicators.note: consuming means swallowing, so the word for an agent takes the upturned drink inside it

parts.note: a spy is a secret agent

indicators.note: north is the top of the grid in a down entry, so the drink is written from the bottom upwards

parts.note: port is a fortified wine from Portugal

explanation.surface: A grumpy operative downs a glass on the journey up the country.
explanation.walkthrough: In the surface it is the agent who is 'heading north'; in the wordplay only the drink travels, climbing the grid to give TROP, which 'consuming' then tucks inside the agent.
explanation.definitionFit: It is British informal for bad-tempered and awkward to deal with, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Excellent reserve embracing exercise? Right

indicators.note: embracing means putting arms round, so the word for a reserve wraps round what follows it

parts.note: a sub, short for substitute, is a reserve player in a sports team
PE is physical education, the school lesson of exercise

explanation.surface: A first-rate substitute is confirmed to be taking up a fitness routine.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and 'Right' pose as a question and its reply, but 'Right' is one more letter in the embrace: 'embracing' takes in both PE, the school exercise lesson, and that letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are adjectives of the highest praise, meaning outstandingly good, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Request European entertainment in us city

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for European, as in EU

indicators.note: in tells us the word for an entertainment goes inside the abbreviated city

parts.note: NY is New York, America's largest city, in its usual abbreviation
a treat is an outing or entertainment laid on to give someone pleasure

explanation.surface: Someone is told to ask for a continental-style show while in an American town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Request' reads as a command but is a noun here. 'European entertainment' is not one unit either: 'in' puts only the entertainment inside the city, and the letter for European stays in front.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an earnest plea or petition, a more urgent synonym for something asked.

clue.text: Sweet scent of feet? Not entirely!

indicators.note: not entirely means only part of the phrase before it is used, an unbroken run of its letters

explanation.surface: Asked whether feet smell pleasant, someone replies that they do not altogether.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' reads as an adjective for the scent, but it is a noun, the British word for a piece of confectionery; 'Not entirely' takes a run of letters from inside 'scent of feet'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a chewy confection of boiled sugar and butter, an example of what Americans would call candy.

clue.text: Principal among the Romans

indicators.note: among means in the midst of, so the answer sits inside the two words that follow it

explanation.surface: The leading figure in a crowd of ancient Romans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' says the answer lies inside 'the Romans', spanning the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief male character in a story or play is its lead, so the two are near-synonyms in the theatrical sense.

clue.text: Poet extended chap

parts.note: an extended stay is a long one, stretched out in time
chap and fellow are both informal words for a man

explanation.surface: A writer of verse stretched some poor bloke out.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Wadsworth, the American author of The Song of Hiawatha, bore this surname, so he is an example of a versifier.

clue.text: For audience, disclose without permission national symbol

indicators.note: an audience listens, so the word clued next is to be heard rather than read

parts.note: to leak information is to reveal it without authority

explanation.surface: In front of a crowd, someone reveals a country's emblem without being authorised to.
explanation.walkthrough: The vegetable is the national emblem of Wales, worn on St David's Day; 'For audience' says it merely sounds like LEAK.
explanation.definitionFit: This vegetable is the emblem of Wales, so it is an example of a country's badge.

clue.text: Wealthy figure, a good name entertained by end of game

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to have them in, so the word for a game's end takes the other three letters inside

parts.note: mate, short for checkmate, is how a game of chess ends
taken as written
G is the abbreviation for good, as in VG on school work
N is the abbreviation for name, as on forms

explanation.surface: A tycoon with a fine reputation is being wined and dined as the match finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'end of game' looks like a last-letter instruction for E; here it is MATE, the finish of a chess game, and 'entertained by' puts A, G and N inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a person of great riches and influence in business, a tycoon, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Acknowledgement about country residence, we hear

parts.note: re means about or concerning, as at the head of a business letter

indicators.note: we hear tells us the word for a country residence is listened to, not read

parts.note: a seat is a country house, as in the family seat of a landed family

explanation.surface: We are told there has been a formal reply concerning a rural home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' means only the sound of SEAT is used: it matches the ending CEIPT, where the P is silent.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a written confirmation that goods or money have arrived, so it is a synonym in that formal sense.
